# How to Automate Everyday Apps with Zapier and Your AI Assistant

> **In short:** Zapier says you can connect it to an AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Cursor, describe a task in plain language, and have Zapier run it in the background. The setup takes a few steps, and the result keeps working after you close the chat.

You probably have a handful of small jobs that repeat every week: saving meeting notes, copying leads into a spreadsheet, sharing a post to a second app. Your AI assistant can help you think them through, but once the chat ends, nothing happens on its own. This guide shows you how to change that.

## What you need before you start

Let's cover the basics first, so nothing surprises you halfway through.

- **A Zapier account.** Zapier is the service that runs the automations. You create the account on Zapier's website. For plan details, check the official pricing page, because plans can change.
- **An AI assistant that supports MCP.** MCP (Model Context Protocol, a standard way for an AI tool to connect to outside apps) is what links your assistant to Zapier. Zapier's examples use ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, and the company says any AI tool that supports MCP can work the same way.
- **Accounts for the apps you want to connect.** Think Google Drive, Notion, Slack, HubSpot, or Asana. Zapier handles each app's login for you.
- **For Instagram:** Zapier's Instagram for Business integration requires a Business or Creator account on Instagram.

Zapier says it can reach more than 10,000 apps, but you only need the few you actually use.

## Step 1 — Open your Zapier MCP dashboard

Your first job is to give your AI assistant a way to reach Zapier. Sign in to Zapier and find the MCP dashboard. Zapier calls this the Zapier MCP dashboard, and it's where you manage the connections your AI tool uses.

💬 Keep the browser tab open. You'll come back to it in the next two steps.

You'll know it worked when you can see the dashboard with an option to create a new MCP server. You don't need to create anything yet.

## Step 2 — Create a server and choose your AI tool

On the dashboard, click **+New MCP Server**. When asked which client to use, choose the AI tool you want to work with. Zapier's ChatGPT walkthrough, for example, selects ChatGPT as the client.

If you use a different assistant, choose that one instead. The idea is the same: you're telling Zapier, "This is the AI tool that will send instructions to you."

💬 Name your server something you'll recognize later, such as "Weekly work helper." Naming is optional, but it helps when you have several setups.

You'll know it worked when your new server appears on the dashboard and the AI tool you chose is listed as its client.

## Step 3 — Add your first app action

An "action" is a single thing an app can do, like creating a row, sending a message, or adding a document. Zapier's instructions say to click **+Add tool**, then search for the app you want.

1. Click **+Add tool**.
2. Type the name of the app in the search box, for example "Google Docs" or "Slack."
3. Click the app's tile in the results.
4. Select the action events you want the AI to use, such as "create document" or "send message."
5. Click **Connect**, then connect your account for that app when asked.

💬 Start with one action. A good first choice is something low-risk, like creating a draft in Google Docs. You can always add more later.

You'll know it worked when the app appears on your server's tool list with the action you picked.

## Step 4 — Describe the job in plain language

This is the part that feels most like a regular chat. Go back to your AI assistant and explain what you want in ordinary words. Pretend you're giving a task to a coworker.

Zapier's own examples follow this pattern:

💬 "When someone messages our Facebook page, send them a quick reply, then post the message in #social-inbox in Slack."

💬 "Whenever I publish on Instagram, share it on my Facebook Page and add a row to my content tracker."

Your assistant turns your sentence into an automation, which Zapier calls a **Zap** (an automated workflow that runs on its own). The Zap starts when its trigger happens, such as a new message or a new post.

You'll know it worked when your assistant describes back to you what it plans to build, step by step.

## Step 5 — Review what the assistant built

Before you rely on the automation, look at it. Zapier says the agent drafts the Zap, deploys it to Zapier, and shows you what it built. Read that summary carefully.

Ask yourself three questions:

- **Does the trigger match my intent?** The trigger is what starts the Zap. A new Instagram post should start it, not a comment.
- **Does each step go to the right app and place?** Check the channel name, folder, or spreadsheet.
- **Is anything missing?** If you wanted a summary and a follow-up task, both should appear.

If something looks off, tell the assistant what to change in plain words, such as "Post to #sales instead of #general." Ask for a corrected version and review it again.

You'll know it worked when the summary matches what you pictured and every destination is one you recognize.

## Step 6 — Let it run, then check the first results

Here's the part that makes this different from a normal chat. Zapier says the Zap keeps running after you close the chat, even when your laptop is closed. You don't need to keep the AI tool open for it to work.

Wait for the trigger to happen once, such as your next Instagram post or a new meeting transcript. Then open the destination app and look for the result.

Zapier's examples describe a few real routines: saving a call transcript to a Google Drive folder and posting the summary in Slack, or pulling data from a Google Sheet into a weekly report in Notion.

💬 "After my next meeting, check that the transcript landed in the Client Calls folder."

You'll know it worked when the first run appears where you expected, with the right content in the right place.

## Common mistakes (and how to fix them)

**Mistake 1: Starting with too many automations at once.** It's tempting to build five things on day one. If one breaks, you won't know which. *Fix:* Build one automation, confirm it works for a few runs, then add the next.

**Mistake 2: Describing the job too vaguely.** "Help with my notes" gives the assistant little to work with. *Fix:* Name the trigger, the app, and the destination. "When a new Plaud transcript is ready, save it to the Client Calls folder in Google Drive."

**Mistake 3: Skipping the review step.** Trusting the first draft can send messages to the wrong channel. *Fix:* Read the summary from Step 5 every time, and test with a low-stakes trigger first.

**Mistake 4: Forgetting the account requirement.** An Instagram automation won't connect without a Business or Creator account. *Fix:* Check the requirements in the "What you need" section before you start.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: Think about one chore you repeat each week, like saving receipts, logging your reading, or sharing a photo album. Describe it to your assistant and see whether Zapier can run the part you'd otherwise forget.
- **For your business or work**: Meeting follow-ups, lead entry, and social posting are common targets. Zapier's examples include copying leads into HubSpot, creating Asana tasks from meeting summaries, and posting customer messages to a Slack channel.
- **If you're just getting started**: Pick one app you already use, connect it, and build a single low-risk automation. Creating a draft in Google Docs is a gentle first step.
- **If you already use it**: Try a two-app chain. For example, have one automation post a new Instagram item to Facebook and log it in a spreadsheet, then check each destination after a few runs.

## Wrap-up

Zapier says you can connect your AI assistant to thousands of apps, describe a routine in plain language, and let Zapier keep it running after the chat closes. Start small: set up the MCP server, connect one app, describe one job, review the summary, and watch the first run. Your next step is to open your Zapier MCP dashboard today and create one server.
